danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: I Petersborg pågik på den tid en indviklet kamp med større hede end nogensinde i de højeste kredse mellem partierne omkring Rumjántsev, franskmændene, Márja Fjódorovna, tronfølgeren og andre, overdøvet som sædvanligt af hofsvirret. Men det rolige, luksuriøse liv i Petersborg, der kun beskæftigede sig med fantomer og spejlbilleder af det virkelige liv, gik sin vante gang og gjorde det svært, undtagen med stor anstrengelse, at indse den fare og den vanskelige stilling, det russiske folk befandt sig i. Der var de samme modtagelser og baller, det samme franske teater, de samme hofinteresser, tjenesteinteresser og intriger som altid. Kun i de allerhøjeste kredse forsøgte man at holde sig den faktiske situations vanskeligheder for øje. Der hviskedes historier om, hvor forskelligt de to kejserinder opførte sig under disse vanskelige omstændigheder. Kejserinde Márja, optaget af velgørenhedsanstalterne og undervisningsinstitutionerne under hendes protektorat, havde givet ordre til, at de alle skulle flyttes til Kazán, og sagerne fra disse institutioner var allerede pakket. Kejserinde Elisabeth havde derimod, da man spurgte, hvilke ordrer hun ønskede at give — med sin karakteristiske russiske patriotisme — svaret, at hun ingen ordrer kunne give om statsinstitutioner, for det var kejserens sag, men hvad hende personligt angik, ville hun være den sidste til at forlade Petersborg.

Hos Anna Pavlovna (Scherer) var der den seksogtyvende august, selve dagen for Borodinó-slaget, en soiré, hvis hovedattraktion skulle være oplæsning af et brev fra Hans Højærværdighed biskoppen, da han overrakte kejseren et ikon af den ærværdige Sergius. Det blev betragtet som et mønster af kirkelig patriotisk veltalenhed. Fyrst Vasilij (Kuragin) selv, berømt for sin foredragskunst, skulle læse det op. (Han plejede at læse hos kejserinden.) Hans oplæsningskunst bestod angiveligt i at rulle ordene ud, ganske uafhængigt af deres mening, med høj og syngende stemme, vekslende mellem en fortvivlet klagesang og en øm mumlen, så klagesangen faldt helt tilfældigt på ét ord og mumlen på et andet. Denne oplæsning havde, som altid ved Anna Pavlovnas soiréer, en politisk betydning. Den aften ventede hun adskillige vigtige personligheder, der skulle bringes til at skamme sig over deres besøg i det franske teater og stemmes patriotisk. En del mennesker var allerede ankommet, men Anna Pavlovna, der endnu ikke så alle dem, hun ønskede i sin salon, lod ikke oplæsningen begynde, men trak den almindelige konversation op.

Dagens nyhed i Petersborg var grevinde Bezukhovas (Hélènes) sygdom. Hun var blevet pludselig syg få dage forinden, havde måttet melde afbud til flere selskaber, hvor hun normalt var et smykke, og sagdes ikke at modtage nogen, men havde i stedet for de berømte petersborgske læger, der sædvanligvis behandlede hende, betroet sig til en italiensk læge, der behandlede hende med en ny og usædvanlig metode.

Alle vidste udmærket godt, at den bedårende grevindes sygdom skyldtes den ulejlighed, der opstår ved at gifte sig med to ægtemænd på én gang, og at italienerens kur bestod i at fjerne denne ulejlighed; men i Anna Pavlovnas nærvær turde ingen tænke det eller endog lade, som om de vidste det.
»Man siger, den stakkels grevinde er meget syg. Lægen siger, det er angina pectoris.«
»Angina? Åh, det er en frygtelig sygdom!«
»De siger, rivalerne er forsonet, takket være anginaen...« og ordet angina blev gentaget med stor tilfredsstillelse.
»Greven er rørende, siger de. Han græd som et barn, da lægen fortalte ham, at tilstanden var alvorlig.«
»Åh, det ville være et forfærdeligt tab, hun er en bedårende kvinde.«

»De taler om den stakkels grevinde?« sagde Anna Pavlovna, idet hun kom til netop da. »Jeg sendte bud for at høre nyt og hører, at det går en smule bedre. Åh, hun er bestemt den mest charmerende kvinde i verden,« fortsatte hun med et smil over sin egen begejstring. »Vi tilhører forskellige lejre, men det hindrer mig ikke i at sætte pris på hende, som hun fortjener. Hun er meget uheldig!« tilføjede Anna Pavlovna.

I formodningen om at Anna Pavlovna med disse ord løftede en flig af sløret for hemmeligheden bag grevindens lidelse, vovede en ung mand ubetænksomt at udtrykke sin forundring over, at man ikke havde tilkaldt kendte læger, og at grevinden blev behandlet af en charlatan, der kunne bruge farlige midler.

»Deres oplysninger er måske bedre end mine,« svarede Anna Pavlovna pludselig og giftigt til den uerfarne unge mand, »men jeg ved fra pålidelig kilde, at denne læge er en meget lærd og dygtig mand. Han er den spanske dronnings privatlivlæge.«

Og efter således at have knust den unge mand vendte Anna Pavlovna sig til en anden gruppe, hvor Bilíbin talte om østrigerne; med rynket ansigt forberedte han sig tydeligvis på at glatte det ud igen og fremkomme med en af sine vittigheder.

»Jeg finder det henrivende,« sagde han om en diplomatisk note, der var sendt til Wien med nogle østrigske faner erobret fra franskmændene af Wittgenstein, »Petropols helt«, som han dengang kaldtes i Petersborg.
»Hvad? Hvad sagde De?« spurgte Anna Pavlovna og sikrede stilhed til vittigheden, som hun havde hørt før.
Og Bilíbin gentog de faktiske ord i den diplomatiske depeche, som han selv havde formuleret.
»Kejseren returnerer disse østrigske faner,« sagde Bilíbin, »venskabelige faner, der er faret vild og fundet på afveje,« og hans pande blev glat igen.
»Charmerende, charmerende!« bemærkede fyrst Vasilij.

»Vejen til Warszawa, måske,« bemærkede fyrst Hippolyte højt og uventet. Alle så på ham og forstod, hvad han mente. Fyrst Hippolyte selv så sig forundret omkring. Han vidste ikke selv mere end de andre, hvad hans ord betød. I løbet af sin diplomatiske karriere havde han mere end én gang bemærket, at sådanne udtalelser blev opfattet som meget vittige, og han fremkom ved enhver lejlighed med de første ord, der faldt ham ind. »Det kan gå godt,« tænkte han, »og hvis ikke, finder de nok ud af at ordne det.« Og ganske rigtigt, under den pinlige tavshed, der fulgte, trådte den utilstrækkeligt patriotiske person, som Anna Pavlovna havde ventet på og ønskede at omvende, ind, og hun smilede, rystede en finger ad Hippolyte, bad fyrst Vasilij hen til bordet og bragte ham to lys og manuskriptet og bad ham begynde. Alle blev tavse.

»Allernådigste Kejser og Hersker!« deklamerede fyrst Vasilij strengt og så sig om i forsamlingen, som for at spørge, om nogen havde noget at indvende. Men ingen sagde noget. »Moskva, vor ældgamle hovedstad, det nye Jerusalem, modtager sin Kristus« — han lagde pludselig eftertryk på ordet sin — »som en moder modtager sine nidkære sønner i sine arme, og gennem den samlende tåge, der forudser Din regerings strålende herlighed, synger den i jubel: Hosianna, velsignet være han, der kommer!«
Fyrst Vasilij udtalte de sidste ord med grådkvalt stemme.

Bilíbin undersøgte opmærksomt sine negle, og mange af de tilstedeværende så skrækslagne ud, som om de spurgte sig selv, hvad de havde gjort forkert. Anna Pavlovna hviskede de næste ord i forvejen som en gammel kone, der mumler bønnen ved nadveren: »Lad den dristige og uforskammede Goliat...« hviskede hun.
Fyrst Vasilij fortsatte.

»Lad den dristige og uforskammede Goliat fra Frankrigs grænser omgive Ruslands riger med dødbringende rædsler; den ydmyge Tro, den russiske Davids slynge, skal pludselig ramme hans hoved i hans blodtørstige stolthed. Dette ikon af den ærværdige Sergius, Guds tjener og ihærdig forkæmper for vort fædreland i fordums tid, overrækkes Deres Kejserlige Majestæt. Det smerter mig, at mine svindende kræfter forhindrer mig i at glæde mig over Deres allernådigste nærværelse. Jeg opløfter inderlige bønner til Himlen om, at den Almægtige må ophøje de retfærdiges slægt og nådigt opfylde Deres Majestæts ønsker.«
»Hvilken kraft! Hvilken stil!« blev der sagt til anerkendelse af både oplæseren og forfatteren.
Oplivet af den tale talte Anna Pavlovnas gæster længe om fædrelandets tilstand og fremsatte forskellige gisninger om udfaldet af det slag, der ville stå om få dage.
»De skal se,« sagde Anna Pavlovna, »at vi i morgen, på kejserens fødselsdag, vil modtage nyheder. Jeg har en god forudanelse!«

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: In Petersburg at that time, a complicated struggle was being carried on with greater intensity than ever in the highest circles—between the parties of Rumyantsev, the French, Maria Fedorovna, the Tsarevich, and others—drowned as usual by the buzzing of the court drones. But the calm, luxurious life of Petersburg, concerned only with phantoms and reflections of real life, went on as before, and it took great effort to realize the danger and the difficult position of the Russian people. There were the same receptions and balls, the same French theater, the same court interests and intrigues as usual. Only in the very highest circles were attempts made to keep the true difficulty of the situation in mind. Stories were whispered about how differently the two empresses were behaving in these difficult circumstances. Empress Maria, concerned for the welfare of the charitable and educational institutions under her patronage, had ordered them all moved to Kazan, and the things belonging to these institutions had already been packed up. Empress Elisabeth, however, when asked what instructions she would give—with her characteristic Russian patriotism—had replied that she could give no directions about state institutions, as that was the sovereign's affair, but as far as she personally was concerned, she would be the last to leave Petersburg.

At Anna Pavlovna's on the twenty-sixth of August—the very day of the battle of Borodino—there was an evening party, the chief feature of which was to be the reading of a letter from the Bishop sending the Emperor an icon of the Venerable Sergius. It was considered a model of ecclesiastical, patriotic eloquence. Prince Vasili himself, famous for his delivery, was to read it. (He used to read at the Empress's.) The art of his reading was supposed to lie in rolling out the words, quite independently of their meaning, in a loud and singsong voice alternating between a despairing wail and a tender murmur, so that the wail fell randomly on one word and the murmur on another. This reading, as was always the case at Anna Pavlovna's parties, had a political purpose. That evening she expected several important personages who had to be made ashamed of their visits to the French theater and aroused to a patriotic spirit. A good many people had already arrived, but Anna Pavlovna, not yet seeing everyone she wanted in her drawing room, did not let the reading begin but wound up the springs of general conversation.

The news of the day in Petersburg was the illness of Countess Bezukhova. She had fallen ill unexpectedly a few days before, had missed several gatherings where she was usually the star, and was said to be receiving no one. Instead of the famous Petersburg doctors who usually attended her, she had entrusted herself to some Italian doctor who was treating her with some new and unusual method.

Everyone knew perfectly well that the enchanting countess's illness arose from an inconvenience caused by marrying two husbands at the same time, and that the Italian's cure consisted of removing that inconvenience; but in Anna Pavlovna's presence no one dared to think of this, or even appear to know it.
"They say the poor countess is very ill. The doctor says it's angina pectoris."
"Angina? Oh, that's a terrible illness!"
"They say the rivals are reconciled, thanks to the angina..." and the word angina was repeated with great satisfaction.
"The count is pathetic, they say. He cried like a child when the doctor told him the case was dangerous."
"Oh, it would be a terrible loss. She is an enchanting woman."

"You are speaking of the poor countess?" said Anna Pavlovna, coming up just then. "I sent to ask for news, and hear that she is a little better. Oh, she is certainly the most charming woman in the world," she went on, with a smile at her own enthusiasm. "We belong to different camps, but that does not prevent my admiring her as she deserves. She is very unfortunate!" added Anna Pavlovna.

Thinking that by these words Anna Pavlovna was slightly lifting the veil from the secret of the countess's malady, an unwary young man ventured to express surprise that well-known doctors had not been called in and that the countess was being treated by a charlatan who might use dangerous remedies.

"Your information may be better than mine," Anna Pavlovna retorted suddenly and venomously at the inexperienced young man, "but I know on good authority that this doctor is a very learned and able man. He is the private physician to the Queen of Spain."

And having thus demolished the young man, Anna Pavlovna turned to another group where Bilibin was talking about the Austrians. Having wrinkled up his face, he was evidently preparing to smooth it out again and deliver one of his witticisms.

"I think it is delightful," he said, referring to a diplomatic note sent to Vienna with some Austrian banners captured from the French by Wittgenstein, "the hero of Petropol" as he was then called in Petersburg.
"What? What's that?" asked Anna Pavlovna, securing silence for the witticism she had heard before.
And Bilibin repeated the actual words of the diplomatic dispatch, which he had himself composed.
"The Emperor returns these Austrian banners," said Bilibin, "friendly banners gone astray and found on a wrong path," and his brow became smooth again.
"Charming, charming!" observed Prince Vasili.

"The path to Warsaw, perhaps," Prince Hippolyte remarked loudly and unexpectedly. Everybody looked at him, not understanding what he meant. Prince Hippolyte himself glanced around with amused surprise. He knew no more than the others what his words meant. During his diplomatic career he had more than once noticed that such remarks were received as very witty, and at every opportunity he uttered the first words that entered his head. "It may turn out very well," he thought, "but if not, they'll know how to handle it." And indeed, during the awkward silence that followed, the insufficiently patriotic person whom Anna Pavlovna had been waiting for and wished to convert entered, and she, smiling and shaking a finger at Hippolyte, invited Prince Vasili to the table, brought him two candles and the manuscript, and begged him to begin. Everyone fell silent.

"Most Gracious Sovereign and Emperor!" Prince Vasili sternly declaimed, looking round at his audience as if asking whether anyone had anything to say to the contrary. But no one said anything. "Moscow, our ancient capital, the New Jerusalem, receives her Christ"—he placed a sudden emphasis on the word her—"as a mother receives her zealous sons into her arms, and through the gathering mists, foreseeing the brilliant glory of thy rule, sings in exultation, 'Hosanna, blessed is he that cometh!'"
Prince Vasili pronounced these last words in a tearful voice.

Bilibin attentively examined his nails, and many of those present appeared uncomfortable, as if wondering what they were to blame for. Anna Pavlovna whispered the next words in advance, like an old woman murmuring the prayer at Communion: "Let the bold and insolent Goliath..." she whispered.
Prince Vasili continued.

"Let the bold and insolent Goliath from the borders of France encompass the realms of Russia with death-bearing terrors; humble Faith, the sling of the Russian David, shall suddenly strike his head in his bloodthirsty pride. This icon of the Venerable Sergius, the servant of God and zealous champion of old of our country's welfare, is offered to Your Imperial Majesty. I grieve that my waning strength prevents me from rejoicing in the sight of your most gracious presence. I raise fervent prayers to Heaven that the Almighty may exalt the race of the just, and mercifully fulfill the desires of Your Majesty."
"What power! What a style!" was uttered in approval of both reader and author.
Stimulated by that address, Anna Pavlovna's guests talked for a long time about the state of the fatherland and offered various guesses about the result of the battle to be fought in a few days.
"You will see," said Anna Pavlovna, "that tomorrow, on the Emperor's birthday, we shall receive news. I have a good feeling about it!"
